analysis.evidence: הָאָדָם is the subject of וַיֹּאמֶר. The man’s words follow directly, and the first-person suffixes in מֵעֲצָמַי (“from my bones”) and מִבְּשָׂרִי (“from my flesh”) identify him as the speaker.
analysis.morphology: Qal wayyiqtol, third person masculine singular, with prefixed conjunction וַ־

analysis.evidence: In וַיֹּאמֶר הָאָדָם, “the man said,” the definite noun identifies the speaker. His words עֶצֶם מֵעֲצָמַי, “bone of my bones,” identify him as the particular man from whom the woman was taken.
analysis.morphology: Definite article הָ־ prefixed to a masculine singular absolute noun.

analysis.evidence: זֹאת points to the woman, and הַפַּעַם marks the occasion of the man's recognition that she is עֶצֶם מֵעֲצָמַי, “bone of my bones.”
analysis.morphology: Definite article הַ־ prefixed to a feminine singular absolute common noun, used adverbially.

analysis.evidence: עֶצֶם מֵעֲצָמַי means “bone from my bones” and parallels וּבָשָׂר מִבְּשָׂרִי, “and flesh from my flesh.” The man recognizes the woman as his own kin because, as the verse concludes, she was taken from man.
analysis.morphology: Common noun, feminine singular absolute, without prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: bone and flesh: one’s own kin

analysis.evidence: In עֶצֶם מֵעֲצָמַי, the man calls the woman “bone from my bones.” The parallel בָּשָׂר מִבְּשָׂרִי, “flesh from my flesh,” expresses their kinship through her origin from his own body.
analysis.morphology: Preposition מִן (here מֵ־) + feminine plural construct noun + first-person singular possessive suffix ־ַי.
analysis.sense: bone and flesh: one’s own kin

analysis.evidence: וּבָשָׂר מִבְּשָׂרִי, “and flesh from my flesh,” parallels עֶצֶם מֵעֲצָמַי, “bone from my bones.” The man identifies the woman as kin by describing her flesh as taken from his own body.
analysis.morphology: Conjunction וּ prefixed to a masculine singular absolute noun.

analysis.evidence: מִבְּשָׂרִי parallels מֵעֲצָמַי, “from my bones.” The man identifies his own flesh as the source of hers, as the closing words explain that she was taken from man. This shared bodily origin expresses kinship.
analysis.morphology: Preposition מִן prefixed to a masculine singular construct noun with the first-person singular possessive suffix ־ִי.

draft.change: Clarify the use of prefixed לְ in the Genesis 2:23 evidence for the existing “this-one” sense of זֶה.
draft.definition: Used independently, the feminine singular זֹאת can point to a woman present as “this one.”
draft.evidence: Genesis 2:23 places לְזֹאת before יִקָּרֵא אִשָּׁה, identifying the woman who receives the designation.

analysis.evidence: In לְזֹאת יִקָּרֵא אִשָּׁה, לְ marks the person to whom the designation אִשָּׁה applies. The closing לֻקֳחָה זֹּאת, “this one was taken,” points back to the same woman.
analysis.morphology: Prefixed preposition לְ followed by זֹאת, the feminine singular form of the demonstrative pronoun זֶה.
analysis.sense: Points to a person present as “this one.”

analysis.evidence: לְזֹאת identifies the one being named, and אִשָּׁה supplies the designation. The following כִּי clause explains the choice of אִשָּׁה through its wordplay with אִישׁ.
analysis.morphology: Niphal imperfect, third person masculine singular, used impersonally.

analysis.evidence: In לְזֹאת יִקָּרֵא אִשָּׁה, the man calls her “woman.” He explains the designation with כִּי מֵאִישׁ לֻקֳחָה זֹּאת, “because she was taken from man,” playing on the sound of אִשָּׁה and אִישׁ.
analysis.morphology: Feminine singular common noun in the absolute state, without prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: כִּי introduces מֵאִישׁ לֻקֳחָה זֹּאת, “this one was taken from man,” giving the reason she is called אִשָּׁה and linking that name to אִישׁ.
analysis.morphology: Uninflected conjunction with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: In כִּי מֵאִישׁ לֻקֳחָה זֹּאת, the preposition marks the man as the source from whom the woman was taken. The speaker pairs אִישׁ ‘man’ with אִשָּׁה ‘woman’ to explain her designation.
analysis.morphology: Prefixed preposition מִן, appearing as מֵ־ before א, + masculine singular absolute noun.

analysis.evidence: In מֵאִישׁ לֻקֳחָה זֹּאת, “this one was taken from man,” זֹּאת refers to the woman and agrees with the feminine singular verb. מֵאִישׁ identifies the source, echoing “bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh.”
analysis.morphology: Pual perfect, third person feminine singular
